description.narrative: RWI's China program focuses on strengthening Chinese academic institutions in Human Rights components and teaching.
RWI:s ”Human Rights Capacity Development Programme in China” för perioden är i huvudsak ett samarbete med den akademiska sektorn.

The overall objective of the Raoul Wallenberg Institute of Human Rights and Humanitarian Laws Human Rights Capacity Development Programme for China is to strengthen institutions and networks for the promotion and protection of human rights, including gender equality, in China. The interventions intended outcomes are: Outcome 1: Improved human rights education and engagement, including education for gender equality, by key Chinese academic institutions; Outcome 2: Improved capacity for research- based advocacy, including an inter-sectional perspective, amongst academics, civil society organisations (CSOs), disabled people's organisations (DPOs) and government officials. Due to the difficulties associated with the Foreign NGO Law and other developments elaborated upon in the Risk Assessment and Mitigation Plans submitted to Sida, the two other outcomes originally planned under the Programme were deprioritized since 2020, namely: Outcome 3: Institutionalisation of human rights education within the Chinese prosecution system, and Outcome 4: Improved implementation of gender sensitive juvenile justice mechanisms among justice sector stakeholders. Instead, a new outcome relating to "Global China" and its impacts on human rights and the environment was added to the Programme in 2020, namely: Outcome 5: Increased knowledge and more effective engagement addressing China's role in global and regional governance and multilateral issues related to human rights, the environment and sustainable development.

RWI has had fruitful cooperation programmes for two decades in China, both with universities and with justice sector institutions. However, the tolerance and space that existed in China in the late 1990s and early 2000s for constructive engagement on human rights in the form of capacity development, education, research and professional training has been shrinking and diminishing year by year during the last decade. The current China Programme 2017-2022 was planned and implemented in this worsening climate. The longstanding cooperation with justice sector institutions was discontinued in 2018, as the Supreme Peoples Procuratorate (SPP) and the National Prosecutors College of China (NPrC) were no longer able to cooperate with a non-registered foreign organization. The focus of the programme is since on the consolidation of successful initiatives and well-established partnerships in the academic sector, where there is still some space to continue to support education, training and research albeit under great uncertainty, unpredictability and bureaucratic burdens to obtain the activity approvals required by the Foreign NGO Law. As per December 2021, however, Peking University Law School Research Centre for Human Rights (PULS/RCHR) and the Human Rights research Direction for master students that RWI has been supporting at the university since 2004 was suspended for one year by the university authorities.
Since 2018, RWI has increased its engagement on Chinas global role and footprint. A new outcome relating to global China and its impacts on human rights and the environment was added to the China Programme, aiming to address Chinas role in global and regional governance and multilateral issues related to human rights, the environment and sustainable development. In step with Chinas growing economic power and political influence around the world, there is a need and interest among stakeholders to engage in projects addressing the social and environmental impacts of global China and of Chinese investments in the AsiaPacific region. China has furthermore become more active as a development actor and in international organisations, affirming the relevance and importance of RWI promoting international human rights standards and human rights-based approaches to development together with partners in Asia and beyond. Activities addressing these topics have been carried out both in Asia and Europe in 2019-2021, forming part of a contingency plan for RWIs continued work on China while also addressing some of the key human rights concerns and identified needs in the region.
Programme implementation in 2021 was continuously affected by the Covid-19 pandemic. Adaptive measures were put in place throughout the year to secure the implementation of activities in accordance with the workplan. Despite challenges relating both to the pandemic and the increasingly restrictive political and legal context, significant results have been achieved within the Programme since 2017: - Peking Universitys PULS/RCHR human rights master programme is recognized as an established model institution and a valuable resource for human rights learning across China; - There is an increased interest in teaching courses on gender and human rights and business and human rights in China; - There is increased networking and knowledge sharing among Chinese academics, and encouraging examples of an increased voice of human rights educators within China; - Institutionalised and sustainable human rights training courses of high quality are provided by Chinese prosecutor training institutions both at the national and the provincial levels; and Chaoyue Agency is increasingly seen as a leading proponent of juvenile justice reform in line with international human rights standards in China. - Networks of academics, civil society and other practitioners around issues of Global China and how it relates to human rights, governance and the environment were strengthened through conferences and other activities together with China Dialogue and the Made in China Journal. RWI and partners contributed to new knowledge in this area through publication of in-depth, open access articles.
No indicator available - only a description of the activity results is published
